mcqs.q: The colour of clinically healthy gingiva is:
mcqs.explain: Healthy gingiva is coral or salmon pink; redness/cyanosis indicate inflammation.

mcqs.q: Stippling of the gingival surface is a sign of:
mcqs.explain: A matte, stippled surface is a feature of HEALTH; stippling is lost (smooth, shiny) in gingivitis.

mcqs.q: The predominant immune cell in the INITIAL gingival lesion is the:
mcqs.explain: Initial lesion (2–4 days) = PMN infiltration of the sulcular & junctional epithelium.

mcqs.q: Bleeding on probing first appears clinically in which stage?
mcqs.explain: The early lesion (4–7 days) shows erythema + bleeding on probing; the initial lesion is subclinical.

mcqs.q: Plasma cells become the predominant connective-tissue cell from the:
mcqs.explain: From the established lesion (14–21 days) onward, plasma cells dominate the connective tissue.

mcqs.q: The bluish hue of chronically inflamed gingiva is mainly due to:
mcqs.explain: Engorged vessels + sluggish flow → localized anoxemia → bluish hue; RBC breakdown deepens the colour.

mcqs.q: A periodontal pocket is best defined as a:
mcqs.explain: Periodontal pocket = a pathologically deepened gingival sulcus, detected by careful probing.

mcqs.q: A pocket whose base is CORONAL to (above) the alveolar bone is:
mcqs.explain: Suprabony pocket: base above bone (horizontal loss). Intrabony/infrabony: base below bone (vertical loss).

mcqs.q: The enzyme chiefly responsible for collagen breakdown in pocket formation is:
mcqs.explain: PMN collagenase (a matrix metalloproteinase) degrades collagen; fibroblasts also phagocytose fibres.

mcqs.q: Coronal junctional epithelium begins to detach when PMNs exceed about:
mcqs.explain: When PMNs make up >60% of the JE volume it loses cohesiveness and the coronal portion detaches.

mcqs.q: In clinically healthy gingiva the connective tissue is completely free of inflammatory cells.
mcqs.explain: False — a few neutrophils, lymphocytes & macrophages are normally present (steady-state equilibrium).

mcqs.q: The initial gingival lesion is usually clinically apparent.
mcqs.explain: False — the initial lesion is SUBCLINICAL; the changes are microscopic.

mcqs.q: Bone loss occurs only in the advanced (Stage IV) gingival lesion.
mcqs.explain: True — destruction extends into bone and other periodontal tissues only in the advanced lesion.

mcqs.q: In gingivitis the gingiva becomes firmer and more resilient.
mcqs.explain: False — it becomes soft, oedematous and spongy; firmness is a feature of health.

mcqs.q: Careful probing of the gingival margin is the most reliable method to locate periodontal pockets.
mcqs.explain: True — careful exploration with a periodontal probe is the only reliable method.

saqs.q: List the six clinical features used to describe healthy gingiva.
saqs.a: Colour (coral/salmon pink), consistency (firm/resilient), contour (scalloped, knife-edge margin, pointed papillae), surface texture (matte, stippled), tissue resistance to probing (present), and bleeding/pain on probing (absent or slight).

saqs.q: Tabulate the four stages of gingivitis with their timing and predominant cell.
saqs.a: Initial (I) 2–4 d → PMNs; Early (II) 4–7 d → lymphocytes; Established (III) 14–21 d → plasma cells; Advanced (IV) → plasma cells (with bone loss).

saqs.q: Outline the pathogenesis of periodontal pocket formation.
saqs.a: Bacterial plaque → inflammation of marginal gingiva → deepening of the gingival sulcus (gingival pocket) → anaerobic colonisation (motile rods & spirochetes); collagenase/MMP + fibroblast phagocytosis destroy collagen, JE proliferates apically, the coronal JE detaches (PMNs >60%) while the apical part migrates apically → true pocket with attachment loss.

saqs.q: Differentiate a suprabony from an intrabony (infrabony) pocket.
saqs.a: Suprabony: pocket base is coronal to (above) the alveolar bone, with horizontal bone loss. Intrabony: base is apical to (below) the bony crest, with vertical bone loss.

saqs.q: State four clinical signs of an established periodontal pocket.
saqs.a: Bluish-red thickened marginal gingiva; gingival bleeding & suppuration; tooth mobility & diastema formation; localized pain or pain 'deep in the bone'.
